questions.q: What is the recommended way to read a Python traceback?
options: Top to bottom, since the first line always contains the error
Bottom to top — the last line is the actual error, and the lines above show the call stack that led to it
Tracebacks should be ignored and the code rerun instead
Only the middle line matters
questions.explain: Python tracebacks are read bottom to top: the final line names the actual exception and its message, while the lines above trace the sequence of function calls that led to that failure.

questions.q: What does dropping `breakpoint()` into your code do?
options: It permanently stops the program and requires a restart
It deletes the line of code it's placed on
It pauses execution at that exact line and opens pdb, Python's interactive debugger, so you can inspect real variable values
It automatically fixes any bugs found after that point
questions.explain: breakpoint() pauses the program at that line and drops you into pdb, an interactive prompt where you can inspect actual variable values, step through code, or continue execution.

questions.q: What makes the "print() debugging, with intent" approach in this lesson different from scattering print statements everywhere?
options: It avoids using print() entirely in favor of logging
It requires installing a separate print-debugging library
It only works inside async functions
It uses a clear, searchable prefix (like "DEBUG:") and prints a specific targeted value instead of dumping entire objects blindly
questions.explain: The lesson's approach to print() debugging emphasizes being deliberate: a consistent prefix makes debug lines easy to find and remove later, and printing a specific value (like dict keys) is more useful than dumping an entire object.

questions.q: In the async-specific trap example, why does `print(result)` show `<coroutine object call_api at 0x...>` instead of the actual API response?
options: Because `await` was missing before the call_api(prompt) call, so result holds an unstarted coroutine object rather than its return value
Because call_api() raised an exception that was silently swallowed
Because print() cannot display strings returned from async functions
Because the API itself returned the literal text "coroutine object"
questions.explain: Calling a coroutine function without await doesn't raise an error — it just returns a coroutine object. This is a very common and hard-to-spot async bug, so a variable printing as <coroutine object ...> is a strong signal to check for a missing await.

questions.q: Why is it useful to know that forgetting `await` doesn't raise an error in Python?
options: It isn't useful — forgetting await always crashes the program immediately
Because this specific bug fails silently rather than loudly, so recognizing its tell-tale symptom (a coroutine object where a value was expected) is the fastest way to diagnose it
Because Python automatically adds await wherever it's missing
Because this only matters for code that doesn't use asyncio at all
questions.explain: Unlike many bugs that throw a clear exception, a missing await produces no error — just a wrong-looking value. Knowing this specific failure signature (a coroutine object showing up unexpectedly) lets you diagnose it quickly instead of chasing the wrong lead.
